_meta.citation_format: chNNN#pMM or chNNN#pMM-pNN, per bible/WRITE_RULES.md section 2
_meta.scope: All 12 chapters of Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, read faithfully from the source text; no realistic-adaptation decisions made here (see realistic_adaptation_flags)
_meta.id_scheme: evNNNN, book-wide unique, assigned in reading order
_meta.note_on_importance: major/minor/background reflects plot weight only; main-line vs. sub-line ownership belongs to 01-story/story-structure, not this file

events.location: the bank beside her sister -> the field -> the rabbit-hole under the hedge
events.cause: Alice is bored and drowsy, sitting idle on the bank with nothing to do.
events.process: A White Rabbit with pink eyes runs close by talking to itself, then takes a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket; burning with curiosity, Alice runs after it across the field.
events.result: She sees it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge and follows it in, without thinking how she will get out again.

events.location: the rabbit-hole tunnel, dipping into a very deep well
events.cause: The rabbit-hole runs straight for a while then suddenly dips into a very deep well.
events.process: Alice falls slowly, with time to look at cupboards, bookshelves, maps and an empty marmalade jar on the walls, and to muse aloud about the centre of the earth, Antipathies, and her cat Dinah.
events.result: She lands unhurt, thump, on a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall is over.

events.location: a long, low hall lit by hanging lamps, with a glass table and a curtained little door
events.cause: Alice sees the White Rabbit still ahead of her, hurrying down a passage, and chases it.
events.process: She loses the Rabbit around a corner and finds herself in a long, low hall with locked doors all round; a glass table holds a tiny golden key that fits a fifteen-inch door behind a curtain, opening onto a lovely garden.
events.result: She cannot fit through the tiny door even with her head, and has no way yet to get into the garden.

events.location: the long, low hall, at the glass table
events.cause: Alice wants a way to shrink small enough to pass through the little door.
events.process: She finds a bottle labelled "DRINK ME" on the table, checks it is not marked poison, and drinks it; she shrinks to ten inches, but then finds she has left the golden key on the table and cannot climb up to reach it.
events.result: She is now the right size for the door but locked out of it, and sits down and cries.

events.location: the long, low hall, at the glass table
events.cause: Alice scolds herself for crying and looks for another way in; she finds a small cake in a glass box under the table, marked "EAT ME" in currants.
events.process: Reasoning that eating it must make her either larger (to reach the key) or smaller (to creep under the door), she eats the whole cake.
events.result: No change is noticed at first; the effect is delayed and only takes hold at the start of the next chapter.

events.location: the long, low hall, at the glass table
events.cause: Delayed effect of the "EAT ME" cake eaten in ev0005.
events.process: Alice suddenly begins growing, "opening out like the largest telescope," until her head strikes the roof of the hall; she is now more than nine feet high.
events.result: She can now reach the golden key easily but is far too large to fit through the little door into the garden.

events.location: the long, low hall
events.cause: Stuck at giant size and unable to reach the garden, Alice sits down and cries.
events.process: Her tears form a pool about four inches deep; the White Rabbit returns, splendidly dressed and muttering about the Duchess, and when Alice speaks to it, it starts, drops its white kid gloves and fan, and flees. Alice picks up the fan and begins fanning herself while wondering if she has been changed into another child.
events.result: She notices she is shrinking rapidly because of the fan and drops it just in time to avoid vanishing altogether, now about two feet high.

events.location: the long, low hall -> the pool of tears
events.cause: Shrunk small again, Alice finds the little door shut and the key back on the unreachable table; she rushes for the door anyway.
events.process: As she runs, her foot slips and she falls, splash, into salt water up to her chin.
events.result: She realises she is swimming in the very pool of tears she wept earlier while nine feet high.

events.location: the pool of tears, swimming
events.cause: Alice, alone and frightened in the pool, tries to make conversation with a Mouse also swimming there.
events.process: She repeatedly offends the Mouse by mentioning her cat Dinah (who catches mice) and a neighbour's rat-killing terrier; the Mouse recoils and swims off each time, but returns when she promises to stop. The pool grows crowded with other creatures that have also fallen in, including a Duck, Dodo, Lory and Eaglet.
events.result: The Mouse agrees to tell its history once ashore, and the whole party swims to the shore.

events.location: the bank of the pool, ashore
events.cause: The whole party is wet, cross and uncomfortable and needs to dry off.
events.process: The Mouse's dry history lecture fails to dry anyone; the Dodo proposes a Caucus-race with no fixed course or start/finish, and after half an hour declares "everybody has won" so all must have prizes. Alice hands round her pocket comfits as prizes for the others and is herself awarded her own thimble back by the Dodo.
events.result: The party, dry and pleased, sits back down in a ring and asks the Mouse to tell its promised story.

events.location: the bank of the pool, ashore
events.cause: Alice reminds the Mouse of its promise to explain why it hates cats and dogs, via its history.
events.process: The Mouse begins a long, sad "tale"; Alice, distracted by the literal shape of its tail, loses track and interrupts with confused remarks ("a knot," "the fifth bend").
events.result: The offended Mouse gets up and walks away despite pleas from Alice and the others, leaving the story unfinished.

events.location: the bank of the pool, ashore
events.cause: Missing the Mouse, Alice says aloud that she wishes her cat Dinah were there to fetch it back.
events.process: The Lory asks who Dinah is; Alice explains Dinah is an excellent mouse- and bird-catcher. The remark alarms the party, and the birds and animals leave one by one on various pretexts (the Magpie wraps up against the night air, the Canary calls its children to bed, and so on).
events.result: Alice is left entirely alone on the bank.

events.location: the bank of the pool, ashore
events.cause: Alone and low-spirited after everyone has left, Alice regrets mentioning Dinah and begins to cry again.
events.process: She hears a little pattering of footsteps approaching in the distance and looks up eagerly, half hoping the Mouse has changed its mind.
events.result: The footsteps turn out to belong to the White Rabbit, revealed at the start of the next chapter.

events.location: open ground where the great hall had been -> the White Rabbit's house
events.cause: The White Rabbit is searching anxiously for its lost fan and gloves (dropped fleeing Alice in ev0007), fearing the Duchess's wrath; the great hall with the glass table has meanwhile vanished completely, unexplained in the source.
events.process: The Rabbit spots Alice and, mistaking her for its housemaid "Mary Ann," orders her to run home and fetch a fan and gloves. Frightened, Alice obeys without correcting the mistake and finds a neat little house marked "W. RABBIT."
events.result: She goes in and hurries upstairs looking for the items, afraid of meeting the real Mary Ann.

events.location: a tidy little room in the White Rabbit's house
events.cause: Alice, curious what will happen since "something interesting is sure to happen" whenever she eats or drinks, and wanting to grow large again, drinks from an unlabelled bottle near the looking-glass after finding the fan and gloves.
events.process: She grows rapidly: first her head presses the ceiling, then she must kneel, then lie down with an elbow against the door, and finally put one arm out the window and one foot up the chimney.
events.result: She becomes hopelessly wedged inside the small room, unable to move, with no apparent way out.

events.location: the White Rabbit's house, Alice's arm out the window / foot up the chimney; the yard and roof outside
events.cause: The Rabbit returns and tries to get into its own house, discovering Alice's giant arm blocking the window.
events.process: Alice snatches at the air and knocks the Rabbit into a cucumber-frame; a crowd (including Pat and Bill the Lizard) is summoned with ladders; they debate burning the house down, then send Bill down the chimney, whom Alice kicks back out; the crowd throws a shower of pebbles through the window, which turn into little cakes as they land on the floor.
events.result: Alice notices the pebbles have become cakes and gets the idea that eating one, since she cannot grow larger, must make her smaller.

events.location: the White Rabbit's house -> outside, past the waiting crowd -> a thick wood
events.cause: Alice eats one of the pebble-cakes on the idea that it must shrink her.
events.process: She shrinks small enough to run out through the door, past a crowd of animals and birds (including the injured Bill being tended by two guinea-pigs) into a thick wood; there an enormous, friendly puppy tries to play with her, and she dodges it around a great thistle until it tires.
events.result: She escapes, safe but exhausted and still tiny, in the wood.

events.location: the wood, among flowers and grass; a large mushroom about Alice's height
events.cause: Alice needs to find something to eat or drink to grow back to her right size.
events.process: Resting against a buttercup, she searches the flowers and grass, then notices a large mushroom about her own height and peers over its edge.
events.result: Her eyes meet those of a large blue Caterpillar sitting on top, quietly smoking a hookah.

events.location: atop the mushroom
events.cause: The Caterpillar demands to know who Alice is.
events.process: Alice struggles to explain her repeated size changes and confused sense of identity in a testy, circular exchange; the Caterpillar tells her to recite "You are old, Father William," but the words come out garbled and altered from what she intended.
events.result: The Caterpillar declares the recitation "wrong from beginning to end."

events.location: atop the mushroom
events.cause: Alice admits she would like to be a little larger than her current three inches.
events.process: The Caterpillar, initially offended, eventually explains that one side of the mushroom will make her grow taller and the other shorter, without saying which side is which, then crawls away out of sight.
events.result: Alice is left alone with the mushroom and an unsolved riddle about its two sides.

events.location: at the mushroom
events.cause: Alice needs to determine which side of the round mushroom does what.
events.process: She stretches her arms around it and breaks off a bit from each side; nibbling the right-hand piece first, she feels a violent blow as her chin strikes her foot, and hurriedly eats some of the left-hand piece to counteract the sudden shrinking.
events.result: The left-hand piece's effect plays out into the next scene, overshooting far past her normal size.

events.location: above the treetops of the wood; the Pigeon's nest in the highest tree
events.cause: The left-hand mushroom piece eaten in ev0021 overshoots.
events.process: Alice's neck shoots up like a stalk above the treetops; a Pigeon attacks her, screaming "Serpent!" and accusing her of coming to eat its eggs; Alice insists she is a little girl, but the Pigeon argues that since little girls also eat eggs, they must be a kind of serpent too.
events.result: Flustered, Alice nibbles alternately at both mushroom pieces in her hands until she returns to her usual height.

events.location: an open place with a little house about four feet high
events.cause: Back at her normal height, Alice comes upon a small house and does not want to frighten its occupants by approaching at full size.
events.process: She deliberately nibbles the right-hand mushroom piece again, shrinking herself down.
events.result: She reaches nine inches high and proceeds toward the house at that size.

events.location: the edge of the wood facing the little house
events.cause: Alice, now nine inches high, hides at the wood's edge near the little house.
events.process: She watches a Fish-Footman deliver a huge letter to a Frog-Footman: "From the Queen. An invitation for the Duchess to play croquet." Both bow low and their curled hair tangles together, making Alice laugh and have to stifle it.
events.result: The Fish-Footman leaves; the Frog-Footman sits on the ground staring stupidly at the sky.

events.location: the door of the little house
events.cause: Alice wants to get into the house to see about the invitation and the noise inside.
events.process: She knocks, but the Frog-Footman argues circularly that knocking is useless (they are on the same side of the door, and the noise inside is too loud to be heard anyway) and refuses to say plainly whether she is even meant to get in.
events.result: Giving up on talking to him, Alice opens the door herself and goes in.

events.location: a large, smoky kitchen inside the little house
events.cause: Alice enters the house and finds the kitchen full of pepper-smoke.
events.process: The Duchess nurses a howling, sneezing baby while the cook stirs a cauldron of soup; Alice asks about the grinning cat ("a Cheshire cat") and is rebuffed rudely by the Duchess. The cook begins hurling pots, pans and fire-irons at the Duchess and baby; the Duchess sings a rough lullaby while violently shaking the child, then announces she must leave to play croquet with the Queen and flings the baby at Alice before rushing out (the cook throws a frying-pan after her).
events.result: Alice is left alone in the kitchen holding the baby.

events.location: the kitchen -> the open air near the wood
events.cause: Alice fears the household will harm the baby if she leaves it behind, so she carries it outside.
events.process: The oddly-shaped baby keeps grunting, its nose growing more snout-like and its eyes smaller; Alice warns it not to turn into a pig, but it fully becomes one.
events.result: She sets it down and it trots away contentedly into the wood; she reflects it makes "a rather handsome pig."

events.location: a bough of a tree near the wood; later a branch closer to the March Hare's house
events.cause: Just after the baby-pig departs, Alice sights the Cheshire Cat sitting in a tree.
events.process: She asks which way to go; the Cat says it doesn't matter without a destination, then describes the nearby Hatter and March Hare as both mad, and argues (via growling/purring and tail-wagging logic) that it and Alice are mad too. It confirms it will be at the Queen's croquet game, then vanishes and reappears twice, finally fading away slowly, ending with only its grin left behind.
events.result: Alice, bemused ("a grin without a cat!"), walks on toward the March Hare's house, growing to about two feet high as she nears it.

events.location: a table set out under a tree in front of the March Hare's house
events.cause: Alice arrives at the tea party already in progress.
events.process: The March Hare, Hatter and sleeping Dormouse crowd one corner and cry "No room!"; Alice sits down anyway. The Hatter comments rudely on her hair, then asks his unanswerable riddle, "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?", sparking a circular argument about "saying what you mean" versus "meaning what you say."
events.result: No one can answer the riddle and the conversation stalls.

events.location: the tea table
events.cause: The Hatter checks his watch, which tells the day of the month but not the time, and is "two days wrong."
events.process: After bickering over "the best butter" gumming up the watch's works, the Hatter explains that he quarrelled with "Time" itself after botching a song at the Queen's concert last March, so Time now refuses to move the clock past six.
events.result: It is established that it is permanently tea-time, which is why so many tea-things are laid out and the party must keep moving round the table to clean cups.

events.location: the tea table
events.cause: The March Hare proposes a change of subject and asks Alice for a story; unable to think of one, they wake the Dormouse instead.
events.process: The Dormouse tells of three sisters living on treacle at the bottom of a well, learning to draw "everything that begins with an M"; Alice keeps interrupting with logical objections, and the party shifts seats mid-story in a "clean cup" ritual. After the Hatter snaps "Then you shouldn't talk," Alice cannot bear it any longer.
events.result: She gets up in disgust and walks off, vowing never to return; the last she sees, the other two are trying to put the Dormouse into the teapot.

events.location: the wood; a tree with a door -> the long hall -> the little passage -> the beautiful garden
events.cause: Walking away from the tea party, Alice notices a tree with a door leading into it and goes in.
events.process: She finds herself once more by the little glass table; this time she unlocks the garden door with the golden key first, then nibbles the mushroom piece kept in her pocket down to about a foot high, then walks down the passage.
events.result: She finally enters the beautiful garden, resolving the goal first set in ev0003-ev0005.

events.location: near the entrance of the garden, at a large rose-tree
events.cause: Alice enters the garden and comes upon a rose-tree near the entrance.
events.process: She overhears the card-gardeners Two, Five and Seven arguing and blaming each other for splashed paint; Two explains they planted a white rose-tree by mistake where a red one should be, and fear beheading if the Queen finds out, so they are painting the white roses red.
events.result: Five spots the Queen's procession approaching and all three gardeners fling themselves flat on their faces.

events.location: at the rose-tree, the royal procession halting opposite Alice
events.cause: The royal procession (soldiers, courtiers, royal children, guests including the White Rabbit, the Knave carrying the crown, and the King and Queen of Hearts) reaches the rose-tree.
events.process: The Queen interrogates Alice and demands to know who the flat gardeners are; Alice refuses to be intimidated and answers "It's no business of mine." The Queen screams "Off with her head!" but Alice retorts "Nonsense!" and the Queen falls silent. The Queen then examines the roses and orders the three gardeners beheaded; they run to Alice, who hides them in a large flower-pot before the soldiers can find them.
events.result: The soldiers report the gardeners' heads gone (satisfying the Queen without the gardeners actually being harmed); the pleased Queen invites Alice to join the croquet game, which she accepts.

events.location: walking in the procession toward the croquet-ground
events.cause: The procession moves on toward the croquet-ground with the Rabbit walking beside Alice.
events.process: The Rabbit nervously remarks on the weather, then whispers that the Duchess is under sentence of execution.
events.result: Alice learns the reason: the Duchess boxed the Queen's ears after arriving late.

events.location: the croquet-ground, all ridges and furrows
events.cause: The Queen orders everyone to their places to begin the game.
events.process: The absurd croquet game begins with live hedgehogs as balls, live flamingoes as mallets, and soldiers bent double as arches; hedgehogs uncurl and crawl away, arches wander off, and players play out of turn, quarrelling and fighting over hedgehogs.
events.result: The Queen rages, stamping about and ordering beheadings roughly once a minute; Alice grows anxious that she could fall foul of the Queen at any moment.

events.location: the croquet-ground
events.cause: Looking for an escape from the chaotic game, Alice notices the Cheshire Cat's grin appearing in the air.
events.process: She converses with the Cat about the unfair game and the Queen, careful to praise the Queen once she notices her listening. The King, unnerved by the disembodied Cat's head, demands the Queen have it removed; the Queen's stock answer is "Off with his head!"
events.result: The King hurries off to fetch the executioner himself.

events.location: elsewhere on the croquet-ground, then back around the Cheshire Cat's head
events.cause: Alice's hedgehog is fighting another hedgehog and her flamingo has wandered off; she goes to retrieve them while the beheading dispute unfolds elsewhere.
events.process: Having caught her flamingo, she returns to find a crowd gathered in dispute: the executioner argues you cannot cut off a head without a body attached, the King argues anything with a head can be beheaded, and the Queen threatens to execute everybody if the matter isn't settled at once. Alice suggests asking the Duchess, the cat's owner, who is fetched from prison.
events.result: By the time the Duchess arrives, the Cat's head has vanished entirely; the King and executioner run about looking for it while the rest return to the game, and the dispute is never resolved.

events.location: walking together on the croquet-ground while the game goes on
events.cause: The Duchess, now apparently free and affectionate, links arms with Alice and walks off with her (the source never shows how her death sentence from ev0035 was lifted -- see broken_chains).
events.process: The Duchess presses close, digging her sharp chin into Alice's shoulder and forcing a strained "moral" out of everything Alice says. The Queen suddenly appears, arms folded, frowning, and gives the Duchess an ultimatum: "either you or your head must be off."
events.result: The Duchess vanishes instantly rather than argue; Alice, frightened, follows the Queen back to the croquet-ground.

events.location: the croquet-ground
events.cause: The Queen returns with Alice to the abandoned game.
events.process: The game resumes; the Queen never stops quarrelling and shouting for beheadings; soldiers guarding sentenced prisoners can no longer serve as arches, so the game gradually collapses. After about half an hour, only the King, Queen and Alice remain unsentenced.
events.result: Out of breath, the Queen asks Alice if she has seen the Mock Turtle and decides to take her to hear his history; as they leave, the King quietly tells the crowd "You are all pardoned," to Alice's relief.

events.location: where the Gryphon lies asleep in the sun
events.cause: The Queen wants to return to overseeing executions and delegates Alice's introduction to the Mock Turtle to a sleeping Gryphon.
events.process: She orders the Gryphon to take Alice to hear the Mock Turtle's history and leaves. Once the Queen is out of earshot, the Gryphon chuckles and reveals that the executions are never actually carried out ("it's all her fancy... they never executes nobody").
events.result: This retroactively reframes every beheading threat in the story so far as empty bluster; the Gryphon leads Alice onward.

events.location: a little ledge of rock where the Mock Turtle sits
events.cause: The Gryphon leads Alice to the sorrowful Mock Turtle, who is willing to tell his history.
events.process: The Mock Turtle recounts being a real Turtle once, and describes his undersea school -- taught by an old Turtle called "Tortoise" -- with an odd curriculum (Reeling and Writhing; Ambition, Distraction, Uglification and Derision; Mystery, Seaography, Drawling, Stretching, and Fainting in Coils) and lessons that "lessen" by an hour each day.
events.result: The Gryphon cuts off the schooldays reminiscing and asks for something about "the games" instead.

events.location: beside the sea
events.cause: The Gryphon's request for something about "the games."
events.process: The Mock Turtle and Gryphon describe and then dance the Lobster Quadrille around Alice, singing "Will you walk a little faster"; they explain the whiting/porpoise wordplay, then ask for Alice's own adventures, which she tells from the White Rabbit onward. Asked to recite verses, she again produces garbled poems ("'Tis the voice of the Lobster," "I passed by his garden"); the Mock Turtle then sings the mournful "Beautiful Soup" song.
events.result: The reminiscing and performance occupy the whole scene, ending mid-second-chorus of the song.

events.location: beside the sea -> in transit, running toward the trial
events.cause: A distant cry that "the trial's beginning" interrupts the Turtle Soup reprise.
events.process: The Gryphon grabs Alice's hand and hurries off without explanation beyond "Come on!", leaving the Mock Turtle behind, his song fading into the distance.
events.result: Alice is rushed toward the trial (opening ch011), not knowing what trial it is.

events.location: the court of justice: King and Queen of Hearts on their throne, jury-box, a table with a dish of tarts
characters: twelve jurors incl. Bill the Lizard
events.cause: Alice and the Gryphon arrive at the destination of ev0044's rush.
events.process: Alice observes the court (the King as judge, wearing his crown over his wig; twelve jurors, including Bill the Lizard, writing their own names down so as not to forget them -- she quietly steals Bill's squeaky pencil). The White Rabbit, as herald, blows the trumpet and reads the verse accusation that the Knave of Hearts stole the Queen's tarts.
events.result: The King calls for the first witness before any verdict can be considered.

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: The King calls the first witness.
events.process: The Hatter testifies, still holding his teacup, giving contradictory dates with the March Hare and Dormouse and a rambling account of "twinkling" tea; the King repeatedly threatens him with execution for unclear evidence; two guinea-pig cheers are suppressed by the court officers. Meanwhile Alice notices she is growing larger again, prompting a testy exchange with the Dormouse beside her about her "right to grow here."
events.result: The King dismisses the Hatter, who flees the court without his shoes; the Queen orders his head taken off outside but he escapes too fast.

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: The King calls the next witness after the Hatter's dismissal.
events.process: The Duchess's cook enters with her pepper-box, causing nearby sneezing, and flatly refuses to give evidence ("Shan't"); asked what tarts are made of, she says "Pepper, mostly," and a sleepy Dormouse interjects "Treacle." The Queen shrieks orders to collar, behead, suppress and pinch the Dormouse, and the court descends into confusion getting it ejected; the cook vanishes in the chaos.
events.result: The relieved King tells the Queen she must cross-examine the next witness herself; the White Rabbit then calls the next witness -- "Alice!"

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: The White Rabbit calls Alice's name.
events.process: Alice, forgetting how large she has grown, jumps up so quickly she tips the jury-box over with her skirt, spilling all twelve jurors onto the crowd below; she apologises and scrambles to put them back, including Bill the Lizard, whom she first replaces head-down.
events.result: The King declares the trial cannot proceed until every juror is restored to their proper place; the jurors are put right and begin writing an account of the accident.

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: The jury is restored and the trial resumes.
events.process: The King asks Alice what she knows about the theft; she says "Nothing whatever." He calls this "very important," and the jury begins writing it down, until the White Rabbit whispers that he means "unimportant"; the King corrects himself, and jurors write down both words inconsistently.
events.result: No evidence is established against anyone from Alice's testimony.

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: Alice's continued growth (established in ev0046 and ev0048) makes her towering in the courtroom.
events.process: The King reads out a just-invented "Rule Forty-two: all persons more than a mile high to leave the court." Alice denies being a mile high; the Queen claims nearly two miles; Alice calls the rule invented on the spot and says a genuine oldest rule would be numbered One.
events.result: The King, humiliated, turns pale and shuts his notebook, calling in a trembling voice for the jury's verdict.

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: The White Rabbit interrupts before the jury can render a verdict, citing newly found evidence.
events.process: He reads out a set of nonsense verses of uncertain authorship and addressee. The King reasons that the Knave must be guilty precisely because the verses are unsigned; the Queen declares this "proves his guilt"; Alice objects that no one even knows what the verses mean. The King then forces a self-serving, line-by-line interpretation matching pieces of the verses to the tarts and the courtroom, including a "fit"/"fits" pun that draws general laughter.
events.result: The King again calls for the jury's verdict, treating his strained reading as sufficient.

events.location: the court of justice
events.cause: The King calls for the verdict; the Queen impatiently overrides ordinary procedure.
events.process: The Queen insists on "sentence first -- verdict afterwards"; Alice objects loudly ("Stuff and nonsense!"); the Queen orders "Off with her head!" but nobody moves. Alice, now at full size and fearless, tells the Queen and the whole court they are "nothing but a pack of cards."
events.result: The entire pack of cards rises into the air and flies down at Alice.

events.time_hint: the same afternoon, late in the day
events.location: the bank, under trees, dead leaves falling
events.cause: The flying pack of cards (ev0052) triggers Alice's waking.
events.process: Alice cries out and tries to beat off the cards, then finds herself lying on the bank with her head in her sister's lap, who is brushing dead leaves from her face. Her sister wakes her, noting what a long sleep she has had, and Alice recounts as much of her "curious dream" of Wonderland as she can remember.
events.result: The whole of Wonderland is confirmed, from Alice's own waking perspective, to have been a dream; she runs off to tea, reflecting on how wonderful the dream had been.

events.location: the bank at sunset, Alice's sister alone
events.cause: Alice has run off, leaving her sister alone on the bank as day ends.
events.process: The sister drifts into her own reverie, half-dreaming the Wonderland figures superimposed on ordinary countryside sounds: rustling grass as the White Rabbit, the rippling pool as the frightened Mouse, sheep-bells as rattling teacups, a shepherd's voice as the Queen's shrill cries, and farmyard clamour as the courtroom's noise.
events.result: She pictures grown-up Alice one day retelling these "simple and loving" childhood adventures to children of her own, closing the book on this forward-looking, reflective note.

broken_chains.note: The Duchess reappears free and warmly affectionate at the start of ch009 (ch009#p01), but the source never shows or explains how the death sentence declared over her in ch008 (ev0035: 'under sentence of execution... She boxed the Queen's ears', ch008#p34-p40) was lifted or reconciled. No pardon, escape, or reprieve for the Duchess is narrated between ev0035 and ev0039.

The dispute over executing the disembodied Cheshire Cat (executioner vs. King vs. Queen, ch008#p61-p71) is never resolved. The Cat's head simply vanishes while the Duchess is being fetched, and the source never states whether it was executed, pardoned, or simply forgotten; no later event addresses its fate.

Between ev0013 (Alice alone on the bank in ch003, at the pool-of-tears location) and ev0014 (the White Rabbit re-entering in ch004, searching near where 'the great hall, with the glass table and the little door, had vanished completely', ch004#p01), the source itself flags the setting change as unexplained ('everything seemed to have changed since her swim in the pool') without narrating how or why the hall disappeared.

The court never reaches a verdict on whether the Knave of Hearts stole the tarts (the accusation set up in ev0045, ch011#p10-p12). The trial is interrupted by the flying pack of cards and Alice's waking (ev0052-ev0053), so the accusation's outcome is permanently unresolved within the source.

realistic_adaptation_flags.note: The entire Wonderland narrative (ev0002-ev0052) is retroactively framed as Alice's dream at ev0053, with her sister's closing reverie at ev0054. A realistic adaptation must decide whether to keep the dream frame explicit throughout, treat it as ambiguous, or reinterpret the events as literally real within a realistic register.

realistic_adaptation_flags.aspect: talking, anthropomorphic animals and living-card figures
